lessons.title: The Exposure Triangle, After Dark
lessons.summary: Shutter, aperture, ISO — the three dials that turn darkness into a photograph.
lessons.body:
Every photograph is a negotiation with light, and at night there's very little of it to negotiate with. Three dials control the deal:

**Shutter speed** is how long the sensor drinks in light. In daylight you think in fractions of a second; at night you think in tens of seconds. Long shutters gather starlight — but they also record motion, which is either your enemy (a shaky tripod) or your entire art form (star trails, light painting).

**Aperture** is how wide the lens opens. A low ƒ-number like ƒ/2.8 is a wide-open eye — you want it open at night. Every stop you close costs you double the shutter time or double the ISO.

**ISO** is amplification. It makes a dim capture brighter, but it amplifies noise along with signal. Modern sensors handle ISO 3200 gracefully; older ones get gritty. Noise lives in the shadows — and at night, everything is shadows.

The trade is always the same: more shutter means motion, more aperture means shallower focus and softer corners, more ISO means noise. Night photography is choosing which compromise serves the picture.

Start with the recipe below on a clear night, far from city glow. Take the shot, then change exactly one dial and shoot again. Twenty minutes of that teaches more than any chart.

recipe.note: A solid starting point for a clear, dark sky. Adjust one dial at a time and study what changes.

lessons.title: Why Long Exposure Changes Everything
lessons.summary: The shutter isn't a moment — it's a duration. Learn to paint with time.
lessons.body:
A normal photograph freezes an instant. A long exposure records a *duration* — and duration is where the magic hides.

Water turns to silk because thirty seconds of ripples average into smoothness. Clouds streak into brushstrokes. Stars, which your eye sees as fixed, reveal that the whole sky is turning. And a person walking through the frame with a light source becomes a glowing line with no person visible at all — that's light painting, and it's why a flashlight belongs in every camera bag.

The technique asks for three things: a tripod (non-negotiable — the camera cannot move even a hair), patience, and darkness. The camera sees cumulatively; you see instantaneously. Learning long exposure is learning to predict what accumulated time looks like.

Noise is the tax on long exposures. Sensors warm up, and hot pixels bloom into fake stars. Serious night shooters capture *dark frames* — same settings, lens cap on — and subtract them, which is exactly what the Twilightscapes camera's dark-frame tool automates.

Every photograph in this app carries its recipe — open any photo's info panel and you'll see the exposure that made it. Steal those numbers freely. That's what they're there for.

recipe.note: The exact settings behind many of the photographs in this app — check any photo's info panel for its recipe.

lessons.title: Star Trails vs. the Milky Way
lessons.summary: Pinpoint stars or circles of light? One number decides — the 500 rule.
lessons.body:
The sky rotates — fifteen degrees every hour. Your shutter decides whether that rotation reads as **pinpoint stars** or **trails of light**, and both are gorgeous, but you must choose.

**For pinpoint stars** (the Milky Way as your eye imagines it): keep the shutter short enough that the rotation doesn't smear. The classic guide is the **500 rule** — divide 500 by your lens's focal length. A 24mm lens: 500 ÷ 24 ≈ 20 seconds. A 14mm: about 35 seconds. Go past that and stars stretch into tiny dashes. Open the aperture wide, raise ISO to compensate, and focus at infinity — on a star, magnified, not by trusting the lens marking.

**For star trails** (circles sweeping around the pole star): you want the opposite — as much rotation as possible. The old way was a single exposure of thirty minutes or more, which cooks the sensor with noise. The modern way is **stacking**: dozens or hundreds of shorter exposures blended so trails connect while noise averages away. It's the approach the Twilightscapes camera is built around — start a stack, watch the trails accumulate live on screen, and stop when the circles satisfy you.

Face north to circle the trails around Polaris; face south and they arc like rainfall. And the Milky Way's bright core is a seasonal guest — roughly April through September in the northern hemisphere, hiding behind the sun the rest of the year. Plan accordingly.

recipe.note: 500 ÷ 24mm ≈ 20 seconds — the longest shutter that keeps stars as points on a 24mm lens.
